title: IELTS Speaking — Practice Test 1
topics: A conversation that changed your mind

questions: Tell me about the first hour of your day — what does it usually look like?
Is there anything you always do in the morning, even when you're in a hurry?
Would you say you're more productive earlier or later in the day? Why might that be?
Has your morning routine changed much compared with a few years ago?
If you could change one thing about your mornings, what would it be?
When you need to find a place you've never been to, what do you usually do?
Have you ever got properly lost somewhere? What happened?
Do you prefer following a map yourself or just asking someone for directions? Why?
Do you think people of your parents' generation find their way around differently from you?
Now that phones give us directions, do you think people will lose the ability to navigate by themselves?

part2.title: Describe a conversation that changed the way you think about something.
bullets: who you had this conversation with
where and when it took place
what you believed before it happened
part2.explain: and explain how this conversation changed your thinking, and whether that change has lasted.
followups: Do you still talk to that person regularly?
Is that kind of conversation rare for you, or does it happen quite often?
Did you tell them, then or later, that they'd changed your mind?

part3.q: Why do you think some conversations stay with people for years, while most are forgotten within a day?
followups: Can you give an example of the kind of conversation that tends to stick?
Is it the ideas that make them memorable, or the person and the moment?

part3.q: Do you think people generally change their opinions because of arguments and evidence, or for other reasons?
followups: What other reasons might there be?
Would that be true for important beliefs as well as small preferences?

part3.q: Some people say we listen in order to reply rather than to understand. Is that a fair description of how most people have discussions?
followups: Why do you think that happens?
Is it worse in online discussions than face to face?

part3.q: How is disagreeing with someone online different from disagreeing with them in person?
followups: What could be the consequences of that difference?
Does anonymity make this better or worse?

part3.q: In what ways do the people around us shape our opinions without us noticing?
followups: Can you give an example?
Is that influence stronger when we're younger?

part3.q: Do schools teach young people how to disagree well? Should they?
followups: What would that actually look like in a classroom?
Who else, apart from schools, has a responsibility here?

part3.q: Is it becoming easier or harder for people in your country to hear views that differ from their own?
followups: What role does technology play in that?
How might that differ between generations?

part3.q: Some argue that admitting you've changed your mind is seen as weakness, especially for public figures. Why might that perception exist, and is it justified?
followups: What might make societies more tolerant of people changing their positions?
Can you think of a situation where refusing to change your mind is actually the right thing?

part3.q: In what circumstances might the ability to persuade others become a dangerous skill rather than a valuable one?
followups: Who, if anyone, should set limits on persuasion — say, in advertising or politics?
Would that be true in every situation?

part3.q: Looking ahead, do you think artificial intelligence that can argue convincingly will change how humans form their opinions?
followups: Would that change be mostly positive or negative, in your view?
How could people protect their own judgement?

fc: Speaks at length about a single conversation without drying up — the Part 2 story flows from context to change of mind without long unnatural pauses.
Uses discourse markers naturally ("funnily enough", "looking back", "to be fair") rather than mechanical ones ("firstly", "secondly") in a personal story.
Self-corrects without losing the thread — a brief "or rather…" and straight back into the idea.
In Part 3, extends answers beyond one sentence unprompted — the examiner should rarely need the follow-up prompts.
Nothing sounds recited: answers respond to the actual question about opinions and persuasion, not a rehearsed speech about 'communication'.
lr: Precise vocabulary for the topic: persuade, reconsider, assumption, perspective, echo chamber, come round to, talk someone into/out of.
Natural collocations — "changed my mind completely", "see it from her point of view", "a heated discussion" — not invented pairings.
Paraphrases flexibly when a word is missing instead of stopping to hunt for it.
Idiomatic language used sparingly and accurately ("it stopped me in my tracks") — one natural idiom beats five forced ones.
Can move from the personal story to abstract Part 3 language (influence, bias, accountability, discourse) without the register wobbling.
gra: Past narrative under control in Part 2: past simple, past continuous and past perfect woven together ("I had always assumed… until she pointed out…").
Hypotheticals and conditionals in Part 3 ("If people only ever heard opinions they agreed with, they would…").
Concessive structures for balanced answers: "Although evidence matters, most of us…", "Even so…".
Relative clauses that add density without derailing: "the friend I mentioned, who I'd known since school, …".
Errors are rare and self-corrected quickly; accuracy never comes at the price of fluency.
pron: Clearly intelligible throughout — an accent is completely fine; swallowed word-endings are not.
Sentence stress lands on the contrast words this test invites: "I used to think X — now I think Y."
Intonation separates the story (lively, varied) from analysis (measured) in a natural way.
Connected speech sounds natural ("changed_my_mind", "sort_of") rather than word-by-word delivery.
Multi-syllable topic words — persuasion, deliberately, controversial — are stressed on the right syllable.

band9.part1: Answer in two to four sentences: a direct answer, then a reason or tiny example. For "Is there anything you always do in the morning?" a Band 9 answer names something specific and real ("I grind coffee before I even check my phone — it's the one thing that makes me feel the day has started properly") rather than a list. React to the question you were actually asked; don't recite a prepared routine speech.
part2: Opening / context — one or two sentences placing the conversation: who, where, when, and why you remember it.
Main description — what was said, in enough detail that the listener can follow the actual disagreement or discovery.
Specific moment — the exact sentence or point that landed; a line of reported speech ("she asked me why I'd never actually tried it") lifts the story.
Personal reaction — what you felt and thought at the time, including resistance if there was any.
Reflection / significance — what you believed before versus after, and how the change showed up in what you later did.
Concluding sentence — one line on whether the change lasted, answering the cue card's final question explicitly.

part3.method: Answer → Explain → Example → Alternative View → Evaluation
part3.question: Do you think people generally change their opinions because of arguments and evidence, or for other reasons?
framework: Answer: take a clear position — e.g. evidence matters less than we like to admit.
Explain: give the mechanism — opinions are tangled up with identity and belonging, so facts that threaten the group are resisted.
Example: one concrete illustration — people rarely change political views after losing a debate, but often drift after moving city or changing jobs.
Alternative view: concede the other side genuinely — in technical questions with low emotional stakes, evidence does change minds quickly.
Evaluate: land the judgement — so persuasion through relationships and experience tends to beat persuasion through argument, which is uncomfortable but useful to know.

mistakes.title: Describing a person instead of a conversation
mistakes.detail: The cue card asks for a conversation. Candidates drift into a portrait of the friend or relative and never say what was actually discussed — which means the deeper part of the card (how it changed your thinking) never gets answered.

mistakes.title: Skipping the 'before' state
mistakes.detail: The fourth bullet — what you believed before — is what makes the change meaningful. Without it, "it changed my thinking" is an empty claim the examiner can't credit.

mistakes.title: One-line Part 1 answers
mistakes.detail: "Do you prefer maps or asking directions?" answered with "Maps." forces the examiner to drag reasons out of you. Two to four sentences with a because is the natural length.

mistakes.title: Reciting a prepared 'technology' speech in Part 3
mistakes.detail: Several Part 3 questions touch on phones and online discussion, and memorised technology essays surface fast. The questions here are about opinions and persuasion — a generic "technology has advantages and disadvantages" answer is off-target.

mistakes.title: Only personal examples in Part 3
mistakes.detail: "My friend once…" works in Part 2, but Part 3 asks about people, generations and societies. Band 8–9 answers generalise — 'many people', 'in most workplaces' — and use a personal case only as illustration.

mistakes.title: Repeating 'change my mind' twenty times
mistakes.detail: The topic invites it. Vary the language: reconsider, come round to, shift my position, see it differently, be talked out of it.

mistakes.title: Fillers replacing thinking time
mistakes.detail: "Umm, you know, like…" before every Part 3 answer costs fluency marks. Buy time in English instead: "That's not something I'd thought about, but I'd say…".

mistakes.title: Not committing to a position
mistakes.detail: Questions like "easier or harder to hear different views?" need a stance. "It depends" with no follow-through is a Band 6 pattern; "It depends — mainly on X, and here's why" is fine.

mistakes.title: Speaking faster under pressure
mistakes.detail: The abstract later questions push nervous candidates into a sprint, and pronunciation features collapse first. Slowing down slightly reads as thoughtfulness, not weakness.

mistakes.title: Treating the AI question as a tech-vocabulary test
mistakes.detail: The final question is about human judgement, not machine specs. Stacking half-understood jargon ("neural networks, algorithms…") hurts Lexical Resource more than it helps.
